analysis.one_liner: Bars states from redrawing congressional maps mid-decade and requires independent citizen commissions to draw them instead.
analysis.headline: The bill has not moved: introduced in September 2025 with zero cosponsors, it sits in the House Judiciary Committee with no vote or hearing scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how congressional district lines get drawn after each census. Instead of legislators drawing maps to favor their own party, an independent commission made up of ordinary citizens — barred from considering party affiliation or where incumbents live — would draft the maps, with public hearings and public mapping software. It would also prohibit states from redrawing maps mid-decade, a practice used to lock in advantages between censuses. A similar version of this idea has been introduced in Congress repeatedly for years without passing.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, whose congressional districts would be drawn without regard to party affiliation or where incumbents live, and who could watch every commission meeting, use public mapping tools, and submit their own maps. Citizens in states that currently let legislators gerrymander — and redraw maps mid-decade to protect a party's advantage — would gain the most, since the bill ends mid-decade redistricting outright. Minor-party and independent candidates would also tend to benefit from less engineer-able districts.

how_it_helps.text: It bans mid-decade redistricting: once a state draws congressional maps after a census, it cannot redraw them again until the next census, unless a court orders a redraw to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act.

It requires every state to draw congressional maps through an independent commission whose members cannot have held office or party jobs for four years and cannot run for Congress until after the next apportionment.
It bans the commission from considering voters' party affiliation or the residences of incumbent House members when drawing districts.

It requires all commission meetings to be public, creates a state website with census data and free mapping software so any citizen can design and submit a plan, and requires public hearings and advance notice before a plan is submitted.

If the legislature rejects the commission's plan, the state's highest court — or a federal district court if the state never forms a commission — must pick or draw a plan under the same neutral criteria.

analysis.who_pays: Party leaders and incumbent legislators, who would lose their ability to draw safe districts for themselves and their party; the bill would also cost federal taxpayers roughly $65 million per cycle in commission funding ($150,000 per House seat), and state legislatures would lose a power they have exercised for two centuries.

drawbacks.text: Commissions are barred from considering voting history or party affiliation (except where needed for the Voting Rights Act or state competitiveness laws), which can unintentionally make districts less reflective of communities of interest and is a real design tradeoff reformers debate.

Taking map-drawing away from elected legislatures is itself a democratic tradeoff: it removes partisan accountability for district lines, and commissions can deadlock or produce plans voters dislike with no elected official answerable for them.

The bill relies on Congress's power over federal elections, which some states and constitutional scholars would challenge as an overreach into state districting authority, and its 2031 effective date means it protects no election before then.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is reasonable and draws on decades of state-level reform experience: banning mid-decade redistricting is the single clearest way to stop gerrymander wars, and independent commissions with open meetings and public mapping tools have worked in states that adopted them. The main costs are real but modest: the criteria ban on considering party affiliation and voting history can make it harder to draw districts that actually elect a second major party's candidates in some states, and taking map-drawing away from legislatures removes accountability to voters if commissions draw poorly. On balance the anti-gerrymandering gains for voters outweigh these design tradeoffs — the larger problem is that the bill has no realistic path, since the majority that would have to vote to limit its own power has not engaged with it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, no cosponsors — so it will likely die when the term ends.

narrative.text: The bill's entire history is two entries: it was introduced on September 17, 2025, and referred the same day to the House Judiciary Committee.
As of the provided record, no other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill would not take effect until after the 2030 census, applying only to redistricting conducted after that census.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, incumbent officeholders and state legislative majorities are better off: nothing has changed, and the power to gerrymander maps mid-decade remains with whoever holds legislative majorities. The 2025 mid-decade redistricting fights it was written to prevent continue unrestricted.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and has been its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (no action taken)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since its referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

against.name: House members generally (0 cosponsors)
against.what_they_did: Not a single member from either party has cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is a Democratic-sponsored redistricting reform with no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan voting pattern exists yet to measure — though similar redistricting commission bills have historically drawn little Republican support.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities
industries.note: The bill strips legislators of the power to draw their own district lines and bars mid-decade remaps, ending the main tool they use to lock in safe seats. This is the concentrated interest the bill exists to constrain.
Banning consideration of party affiliation and voting history in map-drawing reduces the ability to engineer safe seats and the consulting and data work built around them.
States receive federal payments of $150,000 per House seat to run their redistricting commissions, with smaller states receiving nothing under the single-member-state exclusion.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than a year out from the 2030 effective date, the bill is almost certain to die quietly in the Judiciary Committee, as similar versions have in prior Congresses. Redistricting reform through Congress would require broad bipartisan support that does not currently exist, especially while both parties are actively pursuing mid-decade redistricting.
